lessons.name: HTTP/3
lessons.title: Faster Web over QUIC
legend: Datagrams with Initial packets are padded to 1,200 bytes

outro.title: One round trip
outro.desc: The request left after a single round trip

steps.title: Ask for the HTTPS Record
steps.desc: DNS says the server speaks HTTP/3
steps.teach: An HTTPS (type 65) record carries alpn=h3,h2 and an IPv4 hint, so the browser can try QUIC straight away instead of learning it from an Alt-Svc header on a TCP connection.

steps.title: QUIC Initial
steps.desc: TLS starts inside the first UDP datagram
steps.teach: The Client Hello travels in CRYPTO frames inside an Initial packet. Initial packets are protected with keys anyone can derive from the connection ID, so they hide nothing secret, but the datagram must be padded to at least 1,200 bytes so the server cannot be used to amplify attacks.

steps.title: Server Flight
steps.desc: Hello, certificate and Finished in one go
steps.teach: The server answers with its Initial (Server Hello) and Handshake packets carrying the certificate and Finished. Until it has verified the client's address it may send at most three times the bytes it received.

steps.title: Finish and Ask at Once
steps.teach: The client sends its Finished and, in the same flight, the first request on stream 0 using 1-RTT keys. Compare with HTTPS, where the GET waited for a TCP handshake and then a TLS handshake.

steps.title: Streams, Not One Pipe
steps.desc: Loss on one stream doesn't stall the others
steps.teach: The response arrives as STREAM frames spread over several datagrams. QUIC orders data per stream, so a lost datagram only delays the stream it belongs to; TCP would hold back everything behind it.

steps.title: Next Time: 0-RTT
steps.desc: The request rides in the first flight
steps.teach: With a session ticket from this visit, the next connection can send the GET as 0-RTT data next to the Client Hello. 0-RTT data can be replayed, so browsers use it only for safe requests such as GET.

outro.title: Frames, not packets
outro.desc: The switch only reads MAC addresses

steps.title: Who Has This IP?
steps.teach: The laptop knows 192.168.1.20 is on its own subnet but not its MAC address, so it broadcasts an ARP request to ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff. The switch copies a broadcast out of every port except the one it came in on, and records that the laptop's MAC lives on port 1.

steps.title: The Switch Learns
steps.desc: Replies go to one port only
steps.teach: The desktop answers with a unicast ARP reply. The switch learns the desktop is on port 2 and, because it already knows the laptop, forwards the reply only to port 1.

steps.title: Straight to the Right Port
steps.teach: With both addresses in its table, the switch forwards the ping and its reply only between ports 1 and 2. The router's port never sees them.

steps.title: Leaving the LAN
steps.teach: For 8.8.8.8 the laptop uses its default gateway: the IP destination stays 8.8.8.8, but the Ethernet destination is the router's MAC. Every hop rewrites the Ethernet header; the IP header travels end to end.

steps.title: Forgetting Old Entries
steps.teach: A switch forgets a MAC it hasn't heard from in about 300 seconds, so a device moved to another port is found again by flooding. Nothing is configured: the table builds itself from traffic.

outro.title: On the air, sealed
outro.desc: The password never crossed the air

steps.title: Hearing the Network
steps.teach: About ten times a second the access point broadcasts a beacon with its SSID, data rates and an RSN element saying it requires WPA3 (SAE). The laptop lists HomeNet from these beacons.

steps.title: Prove the Password
steps.teach: Both sides turn the password into a point on an elliptic curve and exchange commit messages, then confirm messages. Each proves it knows the password without revealing it, and an eavesdropper can't test guesses offline.

steps.title: Join
steps.teach: The laptop asks to associate, repeating the SSID and the security it chose. The access point answers with an association ID: the laptop is now on the network, but can't send data yet.

steps.title: The 4-Way Handshake
steps.desc: Turn the PMK into session keys
steps.teach: Two nonces and the PMK produce the pairwise key (PTK). Message 3 delivers the group key (GTK) for broadcasts, encrypted. Message 4 confirms; from here every frame is protected.

steps.title: Everything Is Encrypted
steps.teach: The first real traffic, a DHCP Discover, travels inside a CCMP-protected data frame: an 8-byte CCMP header, the encrypted payload and an 8-byte integrity tag. Next stop: the DHCP lesson.

outro.title: Configured itself
outro.desc: No DHCP server, no ARP, no NAT

steps.title: An Address for the Link
steps.teach: Every IPv6 interface gives itself a link-local address in fe80::/64. Before using it, the laptop sends a Neighbor Solicitation for that address from :: to its solicited-node multicast group: if nobody answers within a second, it's unique.

steps.title: Ask for a Router
steps.teach: Instead of waiting for the next periodic announcement, the laptop asks all routers (ff02::2) to advertise now.

steps.title: The Router Advertises
steps.desc: Prefix, DNS and the router's MAC
steps.teach: The Router Advertisement carries the network prefix 2001:db8:1::/64 with the autonomous flag, the MTU, a DNS server (RDNSS) and the router's own MAC, so the laptop never needs ARP for its gateway.

steps.title: Build a Global Address
steps.teach: The laptop joins the advertised prefix to its 64-bit interface identifier and checks the result is unique, again with Duplicate Address Detection.

steps.title: Talk to the Internet
steps.teach: A TCP connection to the web server uses the global address directly. The IPv6 header is 40 bytes with no checksum; routers decrement the hop limit, and there is no NAT rewriting addresses along the way.

steps.title: Open a Connection
steps.teach: A WebSocket starts life as an HTTP connection, so first comes the usual three-way handshake to port 80.

steps.title: Ask to Upgrade
steps.teach: The browser sends a normal GET with Upgrade and Connection headers and a random 16-byte key, base64-encoded.

steps.title: Switching Protocols
steps.teach: The server proves it understood by hashing the key with a fixed GUID (SHA-1, then base64) and answers 101. From the next byte on, the connection carries WebSocket frames, not HTTP.

steps.title: Messages Both Ways
steps.desc: Small frames, either side, any time
steps.teach: Frames from the browser are masked with a random 4-byte key; frames from the server aren't. Either side can send whenever it likes: the server pushes 'Bob joined' without being asked.

steps.title: Still There?
steps.teach: Every 30 seconds the server pings; the browser must answer with a pong. This keeps idle connections open through NATs and detects dead peers.

steps.title: Closing
steps.teach: Each side sends a close frame with status 1000 (normal), then the server closes the TCP connection.

outro.title: Hidden and checked
outro.desc: Encrypted on the way, verified at the source
facts: Which site you then connect to

steps.title: What Plain DNS Shows
steps.teach: A normal DNS query is a UDP datagram anyone on the path can read and even rewrite: your Wi-Fi, your ISP, a café network.

steps.title: Connect to the Resolver
steps.teach: The browser opens TCP and TLS to its DoH resolver exactly as it would to a website. On the wire it looks like any other HTTPS traffic to dns.example.net.

steps.title: The Question, Inside HTTPS
steps.teach: The DNS message is sent unchanged as the body of an HTTP/2 POST with type application/dns-message, so nobody between the laptop and the resolver can read or alter it.

steps.title: Check the Signatures
steps.teach: The resolver asks with the DO bit set, gets the A record plus its RRSIG, then fetches example.com's DNSKEYs to verify the signature. The DNSKEY is itself vouched for by a DS record in .com, and so on up to the root trust anchor.

steps.title: Answer, Encrypted and Verified
steps.teach: The answer returns inside HTTPS with the AD flag, meaning the resolver validated the signature chain. Privacy comes from HTTPS; integrity from DNSSEC.

steps.title: What's Still Visible
steps.teach: Observers still see that you talk to dns.example.net, and the next TLS connection still names www.example.com in its SNI unless the site supports Encrypted Client Hello (ECH).
